comparison: Perfect agreement on low-frequency learning deficits (C50-C52). Both evaluations support that low-frequency learning impairments are not reversed by interventions that rescue high-frequency learning, indicating distinct mechanisms. OpenEval provides detailed statistical evidence while peer reviewers emphasize the remarkable specificity of effects.

Perfect agreement on sex differences (C86). Both evaluations support pooling data across sexes based on comparable impairments in males and females. OpenEval provides specific statistical values while peer reviewers implicitly accept this methodological decision without challenge.

Strong agreement on pre-training rescue effects (C32-C36). Both evaluations support that pre-training restores learning in mutant mice with genotype-specific effects. OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence while peer reviewers describe effects as 'clearly robust' and 'compelling evidence.' Peer review also includes C4 and C11 not evaluated separately by OpenEval.

Strong agreement on selective VOR-increase learning impairment (C24-C28). Both evaluations support the finding with converging behavioral evidence. OpenEval provides detailed statistical analyses while peer reviewers emphasize the task is 'well understood' and results are 'solid.' Peer review also includes C2, C3, C10 not grouped with these claims by OpenEval.

Strong agreement on diazepam rescue effects (C42-C45). Both evaluations support the transient restoration of learning 18-24 hours post-diazepam. OpenEval emphasizes within-subject comparisons and statistical evidence while peer reviewers highlight therapeutic potential and clinical relevance. Peer review also includes C5 and additional claims C46-C48.

Agreement on specificity of diazepam effects (C46-C48). OpenEval separately evaluates the lack of diazepam effects on WT VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning, while peer reviewers group these with the main diazepam rescue findings (C42-C45, C5) as part of the overall pattern of selective effects.

Agreement on OKR adaptation impairment and rescue (C55-C56). Both evaluations support the findings with appropriate statistical evidence. OpenEval emphasizes substantial effect sizes while peer reviewers note this strengthens conclusions by demonstrating generalization across LTD-dependent tasks. Peer review also includes C53-C54.

Strong agreement on central saturation hypothesis (C6, C82). Both evaluations strongly support this mechanistic interpretation based on convergent experimental evidence. OpenEval emphasizes the pattern of selective impairments and genotype-specific effects while peer reviewers describe evidence as 'compelling' and results as 'strongly support their conclusion.' Peer review also includes C17, C57, C61.

Partial overlap on convergent evidence from multiple mouse lines (C57, C61). OpenEval evaluates similarity of phenotypes across MHCI and Fmr1 models as supporting enhanced LTD mechanism, while peer reviewers incorporate these claims into broader support for the saturation hypothesis along with C6, C17, C82.

Agreement on selectivity and therapeutic implications (C65-C66). Both evaluations support that rescue occurs without side effects on related functions. OpenEval emphasizes lack of effects on VOR-decrease and baseline performance while peer reviewers note the 'remarkable' specificity. Peer review also includes C59.

Partial overlap on convergent evidence (C59). OpenEval groups C59 with evidence from both mouse lines showing similar phenotypes, while peer reviewers include C59 with claims about selectivity and therapeutic implications (C65-C66).

Divergent evaluation on mechanistic evidence (C70-C71). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the gap in direct evidence and speculative nature of threshold metaplasticity mechanisms. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging the indirect nature of evidence but accepting it as sufficient given technical difficulties of direct measurement. Peer review also includes C73.

Divergent evaluation on generalizability (C67-C68). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting extrapolation beyond cerebellar findings requires additional validation despite cautious language. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, emphasizing therapeutic implications and potential clinical relevance. Peer review also includes C83.

Agreement on therapeutic implications (C83). Both evaluations support that deficits can be reversed through circuit manipulation. OpenEval notes clinical translation requires additional validation while peer reviewers emphasize potential impact on the field and clinical relevance. Peer review also includes C67-C68.

OpenEval separately evaluates acute diazepam effects (C40) showing profound learning impairment when training occurs 2 hours post-administration, contrasting with beneficial effects after recovery. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found, though this supports the overall pattern peer reviewers find compelling.

OpenEval evaluates differential effects on high- vs. low-frequency learning (C60) as supporting two distinct mechanisms affected by Fmr1 deletion. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers accept the selectivity pattern overall.

OpenEval rates theoretical claims about functions of threshold metaplasticity (C7-C8, C77-C78) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are logically coherent but speculative and not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific theoretical claims.

OpenEval rates mechanistic proposals about threshold changes (C79-C81) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are plausible interpretations based on inference but not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific mechanistic claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims about enhanced LTD from prior studies (C1, C9, C15, C64) as SUPPORTED based on citations to previous work that directly measured LTD. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found, though these foundational findings underpin the work peer reviewers support.
